1. Emerg Med J. 2008 Apr;25(4):205-9. doi: 10.1136/emj.2007.050419. Morphine and outcomes in acute decompensated heart failure: an ADHERE analysis. Peacock WF(1), Hollander JE, Diercks DB, Lopatin M, Fonarow G, Emerman CL. Author information: (1)Emergency Department, The Cleveland Clinic, 9500 Euclid Ave, Cleveland, Ohio 44195, USA. peacocw@ccf.org Comment in Emerg Med J. 2009 Mar;26(3):230-1. doi: 10.1136/emj.2008.064576. OBJECTIVE: Morphine is a long-standing therapy in acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF), despite few supporting data. A study was undertaken to compare the outcomes of patients who did and did not receive morphine for ADHF.

METHODS: The study was a retrospective analysis of the Acute Decompensated Heart Failure National Registry (ADHERE) which enrols hospitalised patients with treatment for, or a primary discharge diagnosis of, ADHF. Patients were stratified into cohorts based on whether or not they received intravenous morphine. ANOVA, Wilcoxon and chi(2) tests were used in univariate analysis, followed by multivariate analysis controlling for parameters previously associated with mortality. Analyses were repeated for ejection fraction subgroups and in patients not on mechanical ventilation.

RESULTS: There were 147 362 hospitalisations in ADHERE at December 2004, 20 782 of whom (14.1%) received morphine and 126 580 (85.9%) did not. There were no clinically relevant differences between the groups in the initial age, heart rate, blood pressure, blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, haemoglobin, ejection fraction or atrial fibrillation. A higher prevalence of rest dyspnoea, congestion on chest radiography, rales and raised troponin occurred in the morphine group. Patients on morphine received more inotropes and vasodilators, were more likely to require mechanical ventilation (15.4% vs 2.8%), had a longer median hospitalisation (5.6 vs 4.2 days), more ICU admissions (38.7% vs 14.4%), and had greater mortality (13.0% vs 2.4%) (all p<0.001). Even after risk adjustment and exclusion of ventilated patients, morphine was an independent predictor of mortality (OR 4.84 (95% CI 4.52 to 5.18), p<0.001).

CONCLUSIONS: Morphine is associated with increased adverse events in ADHF which includes a greater frequency of mechanical ventilation, prolonged hospitalisation, more ICU admissions and higher mortality. DOI: 10.1136/emj.2007.050419 PMID: 18356349 [Indexed for MEDLINE]

1. Lancet. 1998 Feb 7;351(9100):389-93. doi: 10.1016/S0140-6736(97)08417-1. Randomised trial of high-dose isosorbide dinitrate plus low-dose furosemide versus high-dose furosemide plus low-dose isosorbide dinitrate in severe pulmonary oedema. Cotter G(1), Metzkor E, Kaluski E, Faigenberg Z, Miller R, Simovitz A, Shaham O, Marghitay D, Koren M, Blatt A, Moshkovitz Y, Zaidenstein R, Golik A. Author information: (1)Assaf Harofeh Medical Center, Zerifin, Israel. Comment in Lancet. 1998 Feb 7;351(9100):382-3. doi: 10.1016/S0140-6736(98)22006-X. Lancet. 1998 Jun 6;351(9117):1731-2; author reply 1732-3. doi: 10.1016/s0140-6736(05)77764-3.

Lancet. 1998 Jun 6;351(9117):1732-3. doi: 10.1016/S0140-6736(05)77765-5. Lancet. 2001 Apr 7;357(9262):1125-6. doi: 10.1016/S0140-6736(00)04271-9. BACKGROUND: Nitrates and furosemide, commonly administered in the treatment of pulmonary oedema, have not been compared in a prospective clinical trial. We compared the efficacy and safety of these drugs in a randomised trial of patients with severe pulmonary oedema and oxygen saturation below 90%.

METHODS: Patients presenting to mobile emergency units with signs of congestive heart failure were treated with oxygen 10 L/min, intravenous furosemide 40 mg, and morphine 3 mg bolus. 110 patients were randomly assigned either to group A, who received isosorbide dinitrate (3 mg bolus administered intravenously every 5 min; n=56) or to group B, who received furosemide (80 mg bolus administered intravenously every 15 min, as well as isosorbide dinitrate 1 mg/h, increased every 10 min by 1 mg/h; n=54). Six patients were withdrawn on the basis of chest radiography results. Treatment was continued until oxygen saturation was above

96% or mean arterial blood pressure had decreased by 30% or to below 90 mm Hg. The main endpoints were death, need for mechanical ventilation, and myocardial infarction. The analyses were by intention to treat. FINDINGS: Mechanical ventilation was required in seven (13%) of 52 group-A patients and 21 (40%) of 52 group-B patients (p=0.0041). Myocardial infarction occurred in nine (17%) and 19 (37%) patients, respectively (p=0.047). One patient in group A and three in group B died (p=0.61). One or more of these endpoints occurred in 13 (25%) and 24 (46%) patients, respectively (p=0.041).

INTERPRETATION: High-dose isosorbide dinitrate, given as repeated intravenous boluses after low-dose intravenous furosemide, is safe and effective in controlling severe pulmonary oedema. This treatment regimen is more effective than high-dose furosemide with low-dose isosorbide nitrate in terms of need for mechanical ventilation and frequency of myocardial infarction. 1. Expert Rev Respir Med. 2012 Dec;6(6):705-14. doi: 10.1586/ers.12.67. Cardiac asthma: new insights into an old disease. Tanabe T(1), Rozycki HJ, Kanoh S, Rubin BK. Author information: (1)Department of Pediatrics, Virginia Commonwealth University School of Medicine and the Children's Hospital of Richmond at VCU, Richmond, VA, USA.

Cardiac asthma has been defined as wheezing, coughing and orthopnea due to congestive heart failure. The clinical distinction between bronchial asthma and cardiac asthma can be straight forward, except in patients with chronic lung disease coexisting with left heart disease. Pulmonary edema and pulmonary vascular congestion have been thought to be the primary causes of cardiac asthma but most patients have a poor response to diuretics. There appears to be limited effectiveness of classical asthma medications like bronchodilators or corticosteroids in treating cardiac asthma. Evidence suggests that circulating inflammatory factors and tissue growth factors also lead to airway obstruction suggesting the possibility of developing novel therapies.

Deutschland. (3)Zentrale Notaufnahme, St.-Marien-Krankenhaus Siegen, Siegen, Deutschland. (4)Medizinische Klinik I, Kardiologie, Angiologie und Intensivmedizin, Universitätsklinikum der Justus-Liebig-Universität, Gießen, Deutschland.

Acute heart failure (AHF) is among the most common causes of emergency department, intermediate care, and intensive care unit admission and remains associated with substantial early mortality despite advances in contemporary therapy. The first 120 min of management are particularly critical, as this period determines not only respiratory and hemodynamic stabilization, but also trigger identification, decongestion strategy, and the foundation for subsequent prognostic improvement. This CME article provides a practical, phenotype-based approach to the early management of AHF. The proposed strategy is centered on the rapid classification of patients according to congestion ("wet" vs. "dry") and perfusion ("warm" vs. "cold") status. Stabilization and diagnostic work-up must occur simultaneously. Early assessment should focus on identifying acute coronary syndrome, clinically relevant arrhythmias, hypertensive crisis, pulmonary embolism, structural heart disease, and infectious triggers. In addition to clinical examination, electrocardiography, blood gas analysis, and biomarkers, point-of-care ultrasound with lung ultrasound and focused echocardiography play a pivotal role in the first-line evaluation. From a therapeutic perspective, early noninvasive ventilation in cardiogenic pulmonary edema, prompt vasodilation in hypertensive presentations, and effective decongestion with intravenous loop diuretics constitute the core interventions. In cases of insufficient response, escalation strategies such as sequential nephron blockade or selective use of vasoactive agents should be considered. Structured reassessment at short intervals is essential to detect persistent congestion, evolving hypoperfusion, inadequate therapeutic response, or overlooked differential diagnoses. The article emphasizes that successful acute management must already establish the transition toward guideline-directed long-term therapy during the first hours of hospitalization, including early initiation of evidence-based heart failure medication once hemodynamic stabilization has been achieved.

Publisher: Die akute Herzinsuffizienz („acute heart failure“, AHF) zählt zu den häufigsten Ursachen für Notaufnahme‑, Intermediate-Care- und Intensivstationsbehandlungen und ist trotz moderner Therapie weiterhin mit einer hohen Frühmortalität assoziiert. Insbesondere die ersten 120 min der Versorgung sind entscheidend, da in diesem Zeitraum die Weichen für Stabilisierung, Triggerdiagnostik, Entstauung und spätere Prognoseverbesserung gestellt werden. Ziel dieses CME-Beitrags ist es, ein praxisnahes, phänotypbasiertes Management der AHF in der Frühphase darzustellen. Im Mittelpunkt steht die strukturierte

Einordnung der Patientinnen und Patienten entlang der Achsen Kongestion („nass“ vs. „trocken“) und Perfusion („warm“ vs. „kalt“). Parallel zur Stabilisierung von Atmung und Kreislauf erfolgt eine simultane Triggerdiagnostik unter besonderer Berücksichtigung eines akuten Koronarsyndroms, relevanter Arrhythmien, hypertensiver Entgleisung, Lungenembolie, valvulärer Ursachen und infektiöser Trigger. Neben klinischer Untersuchung, EKG, Blutgasanalyse und Biomarkern kommt der Point-of-Care-Sonographie mit Lungensonographie und fokussierter Echokardiographie eine zentrale Bedeutung zu. Therapeutisch stehen die frühe nichtinvasive Beatmung beim kardialen Lungenödem, eine gezielte

Vasodilatation bei hypertensiver Präsentation sowie eine konsequente Entstauung durch intravenöse Schleifendiuretika im Vordergrund. Bei unzureichendem Ansprechen werden Strategien wie sequenzielle Nephronblockade oder selektiv vasoaktive Substanzen eingesetzt. Eine strukturierte Reevaluation in kurzen Intervallen ist essenziell, um unzureichendes Ansprechen, Hypoperfusion oder relevante Differenzialdiagnosen frühzeitig zu erkennen. Der Beitrag betont, dass eine erfolgreiche Akutversorgung bereits in den ersten Stunden die Brücke zu einer prognoseverbessernden Langzeittherapie schlagen muss, einschließlich früher Initiierung leitliniengerechter Herzinsuffizienzmedikation.
